Baby & Child

Ventricular septal defect: symptoms, closure and follow-up

Updated: November 10, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hearing that a baby has a hole in the heart can be frightening. A ventricular septal defect, or VSD, can range from a small opening that needs observation to a larger opening that places strain on the heart and lungs. The useful question is not simply whether a hole exists, but how it affects circulation, growth and the next treatment decision.

What a VSD changes in the heart

The ventricles are the heart’s two lower pumping chambers. Normally, the right ventricle sends blood to the lungs and the left sends oxygen-rich blood to the body. The wall between them is the ventricular septum. A VSD is an opening in that wall, present from birth. It differs from an atrial septal defect, which lies between the upper chambers, and from an atrioventricular septal defect involving the central walls and valves.

In a typical VSD, blood passes from the higher-pressure left ventricle toward the right and returns to the lungs. A large flow can overload circulation and cause heart failure, meaning the heart cannot adequately meet the body’s needs; it does not mean the heart has stopped. This usually is not a problem of low oxygen at first. Blue or grey colour is a warning sign requiring assessment.

Size and position both matter

An opening may lie in the muscular part of the wall or near the valves and other parts of the septum. The cardiologist may use terms such as muscular, perimembranous, inlet or outlet. These describe anatomy rather than a complete prediction. The number of openings, their position, the amount of extra blood flow, heart-chamber size and lung pressure all help determine the plan.

Many small muscular defects become smaller or close naturally. Other defects remain open without major symptoms but need monitoring, including for aortic valve leakage, in which blood flows backward through that valve. VSD is a common congenital heart defect, but frequency and closure estimates depend on the population and type studied. Ask what this child’s echocardiogram means rather than comparing millimetres or percentages with another family’s experience.

Why symptoms may appear after the newborn period

A small VSD may cause no symptoms and be found because a clinician hears a murmur, an extra sound made by blood flow. The loudness of the murmur is not a reliable guide to severity: a small opening can be noisy. A quiet examination immediately after birth also cannot exclude every defect. Symptoms and examination findings can change as circulation adapts after delivery.

As resistance in the lung vessels falls over the first weeks, more blood may pass through a larger opening. A baby may breathe quickly, sweat or tire during feeds, take less milk and gain weight slowly. Some infants develop symptoms early; others appear well longer. Do not use a fixed age or the absence of sweating as proof that a known large VSD is harmless.

When to get help

Call emergency services for serious difficulty breathing, sudden blue or grey lips or skin, collapse, loss of consciousness or a baby who becomes unusually floppy or unresponsive. Chest pain or a concerning new fast or irregular heartbeat also needs emergency assessment; do not wait for fainting. Follow the child’s emergency plan and the emergency service’s instructions. Do not wait for the next appointment or for every warning sign to appear.

Contact the care team promptly for worsening feeding, new or increasing breathlessness, unusual tiredness, sweating with feeds or poor weight gain. A baby who is becoming unwell needs urgent assessment, even without a confirmed heart diagnosis. These symptoms can have other causes, so they should not automatically be attributed to the VSD. Ask in advance how to reach the team outside clinic hours.

How diagnosis and assessment work

An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to show the opening, valves, chamber sizes and blood flow. It usually provides the main information needed after a murmur or symptoms raise suspicion. Some defects are identified by fetal echocardiography during pregnancy, but a normal pregnancy scan does not exclude every VSD. The clinician also assesses breathing, feeding, growth and other examination findings.

An ECG, chest imaging or other investigations may be selected for a particular question; every child does not need every test. Cardiac catheterization may be useful when pressure measurements or more detailed assessment are needed, especially if pulmonary hypertension is a concern. Ask which findings are reassuring, which need watching and what change would bring the next review forward.

Observation is an active plan

A small defect without important extra blood flow may need observation rather than medicine or closure. The follow-up schedule depends on the type of VSD and the child’s findings. Some small muscular defects eventually need little or no further specialist surveillance after an agreed assessment. Nonmuscular defects may need ongoing checks even when small because complications involving nearby structures can develop.

Observation should have clear review arrangements and reasons to seek help sooner. It does not mean waiting several years regardless of growth, breathing or pressure changes. A large defect can require treatment even when obvious symptoms are limited; high resistance in the lung circulation can sometimes conceal the usual signs of excessive flow. Only the specialist assessment can establish whether continued observation is appropriate.

Feeding support and medicines

A baby working harder to breathe may use more energy and tire before taking enough milk. The cardiac and feeding teams can assess weight trends and create a plan for breast milk, formula or both. Some babies need extra calories or temporary tube feeding. Use the prescribed preparation and feeding schedule; do not concentrate formula, change fluid allowances or add supplements independently.

Medicines such as diuretics may reduce fluid-related symptoms while the team monitors the child or prepares for repair. Other medicines are chosen according to heart function and the individual situation. They do not close the opening. Keep a current list of names and doses, and ask what to do if a dose is vomited or feeding becomes difficult. Do not stop treatment or repeat a dose by guesswork.

When closing the defect is needed

A large VSD causing persistent breathing or growth problems may need repair in the first months of life. Closure can also be recommended because of substantial extra blood flow, enlargement of the heart, pressure concerns or damage to a nearby valve. Being an infant is not, by itself, a reason to postpone necessary surgery until preschool age. Timing balances the child’s anatomy, condition and procedural risks.

Longstanding excessive flow and pressure can damage the lung vessels. In severe disease, flow through the opening may reverse, allowing oxygen-poor blood to reach the body. Closing the hole can then be unsafe rather than beneficial. Timely specialist follow-up helps prevent this situation. Ask what treatment aims to prevent, what the risks of waiting are and how the team will judge whether medicine and nutrition support are sufficient.

Surgery and selected catheter procedures

Surgical repair usually closes the opening with a patch or stitches, depending on the anatomy. The team explains the operation, anesthesia, recovery and possible complications for the child’s situation. A catheter-delivered closure device can be suitable for selected defects, but it is not interchangeable with surgery for every VSD. Position near a valve, the child’s size and other heart differences affect that choice.

Occasionally, complex circumstances require a staged approach, such as temporarily limiting blood flow to the lungs before a later repair. This is a specialist decision, not a routine alternative for every young baby. Discuss risks including bleeding, infection, residual flow, valve effects and rhythm problems with the treating team. A population success rate cannot guarantee an individual outcome or replace that discussion.

Recovery, activity and longer-term care

After repair, follow the team’s instructions about medicines, wound care, feeding and return to activity. Growth and feeding may improve as the strain on circulation reduces, but the pace differs between children. Follow-up checks can look for a remaining opening, valve leakage, rhythm changes, heart function and lung pressure. Keep the planned visits even when the child seems much better.

Many children with a small uncomplicated VSD or a successful repair can take part in normal play and exercise. Restrictions depend on remaining problems and the recovery stage; they are not automatically lifelong, or automatically unnecessary after surgery. Ask for advice that school or childcare staff can follow. Children needing continuing surveillance should have an organized transition to adult congenital-heart care, with their records and treatment history available.

Dental health and infection prevention

Infective endocarditis is an uncommon infection affecting the heart’s inner lining or valves. Good oral hygiene and regular dental care matter. Tell the dentist about the heart diagnosis and any repair, and seek prompt medical advice for an unexplained persistent fever. Do not start leftover antibiotics yourself; clinicians may need blood tests before treatment if this infection is suspected.

Preventive antibiotics are not routinely required before every dental visit or operation simply because a child has a VSD. Certain high-risk heart conditions, previous endocarditis or some residual problems beside a prosthetic patch or device can change the advice. The cardiology team should specify whether protection is needed, for which procedures and for how long. Share that written advice with the dentist and other treating professionals.

Causes, future pregnancies and family support

A VSD develops while the heart forms before birth. Often no single cause is found; genetic and environmental factors can contribute. The diagnosis does not establish that a parent caused it. There is no proven way to prevent every case, but pre-pregnancy care still matters: review medicines and existing conditions such as diabetes with a clinician, and avoid smoking and secondhand smoke. Do not stop prescribed medicines independently.

Genetic counselling may be helpful when there are other findings or a family history of congenital heart disease. Ask whether a future pregnancy needs additional screening. Day-to-day care can also place demands on the whole family: feeding plans, appointments and uncertainty can be exhausting. The cardiac team can help arrange practical or emotional support. Keep questions and important records together so decisions can be discussed clearly at the next visit.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the cardiologist to explain the VSD’s location, blood flow, effect on growth and reason for the next review or procedure.

Keep the agreed feeding and medicine plan, with clear instructions for deterioration and contact outside clinic hours.

Obtain individual guidance on activity, dental procedures and follow-up after a repair or spontaneous closure.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize feeding observations, growth records, appointments and questions for the cardiac team. It cannot interpret an echocardiogram, determine lung pressure or decide when a VSD should be closed.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for serious breathing difficulty, sudden blue or grey colour, collapse, loss of consciousness, chest pain, a concerning new fast or irregular heartbeat, or a floppy or unresponsive baby. Worsening feeding, breathlessness or poor growth needs prompt clinical assessment. Do not change cardiac medicines, formula concentration or fluid plans without the treating team.

Evidence notes updated: November 10, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The effect on blood flow, growth, valves and lung pressure matters more than the word “hole” alone.
  • Small defects may close naturally; large defects can need repair during infancy.
  • Medicines and feeding support can help symptoms but do not seal the opening.
  • Follow-up, activity and dental-antibiotic advice are individual, including after repair.
  • Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, collapse or unresponsiveness needs emergency help.

Frequently asked questions

Can a VSD close by itself?

Some do, particularly small muscular defects. Others persist or need treatment because of their effect on circulation or nearby valves. Keep the agreed follow-up rather than relying on a general closure percentage or waiting for a particular birthday.

Can my child be physically active?

Many children with uncomplicated small defects or successful repairs can be active. Advice depends on heart function, lung pressure, remaining problems and recovery after a procedure. Ask for a specific plan rather than imposing a blanket sports ban or assuming there are no limits.

Could anything during pregnancy have prevented it?

Not every VSD is preventable, and its cause often remains uncertain. Pregnancy planning can reduce some congenital-heart risks through medicine review, management of existing conditions and avoiding smoke. This does not guarantee prevention or imply that a parent caused the defect.

Can an infant have surgery for a VSD?

Yes. A large or symptomatic defect may need repair in the first months. Waiting until a child is older can be harmful in some cases. The cardiac team considers symptoms, growth, blood flow, valves and lung pressure when deciding timing.

Does a loud murmur mean the hole is large?

No. A small opening can produce a loud murmur. Echocardiography and the clinical assessment establish the significance; the sound alone cannot measure severity or determine whether surgery is needed.

Will medicine close the hole?

No. Medicines can ease certain symptoms or support circulation, while feeding support helps nutrition. They do not repair the septum. A defect that needs closure requires the procedure selected by the specialist team.

Does every child need antibiotics before dental work?

No. Preventive antibiotics are reserved for selected situations and procedures. Ask the cardiologist for advice based on the exact diagnosis, repair and any residual problems, and share it with the dentist. Regular oral care remains important.

Can follow-up stop once surgery is successful?

Do not stop appointments on your own. The team checks recovery and any residual flow, valve, rhythm or pressure problems, then sets the ongoing schedule. Some uncomplicated small muscular defects need less surveillance, but that decision should be explicit.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
